newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel clears tax bill hurdle, wants more cuts.
newsitem.headline: Waigel clears tax bill hurdle, wants more cuts.

text.p: Germany's Bundestag passed a diluted 1997 tax bill on Thursday, helping Finance Minister Theo Waigel clear another hurdle in his struggle to get state finances into shape next year for European monetary union.
The lower house of parliament voted through the bill by a majority of 335 to 318, and the measure will now go before the opposition-controlled upper house at the end of the month.

Few changes are expected in the bill before it finally becomes law, but Waigel still has his work cut out to control spending and bring the 1997 budget deficit below the Maastricht treaty limit of three percent of gross domestic product.

"We in the federal government, and I assume that the states will follow, are doing all possible to achieve the deficit criterion of below three percent for 1997 in Germany," Waigel told German Radio on Thursday morning.

Waigel said the federal spending gap to be closed was now down to three billion marks ($2 billion), of which a billion marks would have to be cut from transfers to the Federal Labour Office. The remainder would be spread across all ministries.
Extra transfers of 14 billion marks this year to cover Germany's underfunded unemployment insurance system blew away Waigel's 1996 borrowing estimates -- something he does not want to repeat.

"We know that this cannot happen again next year. We cannot afford it," he said. On top of savings of eight billion marks agreed last spring, a further one billion marks would have to come out of the 1997 social welfare budget, he said.

New data showing a jobless rise to a post-unification high will keep pressure on Waigel to balance the books. Unemployment rose by a seasonally-adjusted 41,000 to 4.04 million in October and the jobless situation is unlikely to improve next year.

Waigel's 1997 deficit target is 56.5 billion marks -- equivalent to 2.5 percent of forecast GDP -- but the exact amount of savings needed will only become clear on Friday when tax revenue estimates are published.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition this week found a way out of an internal row over cutting a tax raised to aid east Germany, and can now focus on finalising the budget for submission to parliament's budget committee next week.
A final budget vote is expected in late November.

Coalition sources said that agreement in principle had been reached on cutting the 7.5 percent solidarity tax by two points in 1998, but the measure would be finalised in mid-December in talks which will also tackle plans for a major tax reform.
In Germany, taxation and spending measures are handled separately, and the tax bill can be blocked by the SPD through its majority in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament.
After hard-fought compromises between Waigel and SPD leaders, the tax bill will now only reduce the taxpayer burden by around 400 million marks, instead of the originally planned 5.6 billion marks.

Waigel defended its key aspects -- including the abolition of an assets tax ruled illegal by the constitutional court -- and accused the SPD of pursuing the politics of envy by trying to keep the tax.
"That is no longer a trump card but a red card for investors and jobs," Waigel told parliament. SPD and Green speakers accused Waigel of handing out a tax gift to the rich.

The Bundesrat will debate the tax bill, which also sets new rules on inheritance tax and raises property transaction taxes, on November 29. But, with government and opposition deadlocked on the issue of tax allowances, the measure is likely to end up in parliament's mediation committee.
